Center. In these particular samples, Route A’s median trip is 16.5 minutes, 3.0 minutes longer than Route B’s 13.5 minutes. The sample means differ much less (16.50 versus 15.58) because Route B includes the unusually long 38-minute journey.
Variability. Route B’s middle-half spread is greater (IQR 5 rather than 3 minutes), and its sample SD is also much greater (7.63 versus 2.39 minutes). Reporting both is useful here: the SD responds strongly to Route B’s high extreme; the IQR focuses on the middle portion.
Shape and unusual features. Route A is fairly balanced around its center. Route B has a pronounced right tail and a large gap from 19 to 38 minutes. With its quartiles, the upper 1.5-IQR fence is 16.5+1.5(5)=2416.5+1.5(5)=24 minutes, so 38 is flagged as a potential outlier by this convention. An unusual value should be investigated, not automatically deleted.
Conclusion supported by these data: Route B has the lower median journey time but noticeably greater variability in the two samples. We have not established that one route causes faster travel, that all B trips are shorter, or that the observed differences hold identically for the entire population.


Why the reported IQRs and the 1.5-IQR fence? — Definition and convention


The IQR is defined as the upper quartile minus the lower quartile: Route A has 18−15=318-15=3 minutes and Route B has 16.5−11.5=516.5-11.5=5 minutes. The upper screening fence adds 1.5 times the IQR to the third quartile, giving 16.5+1.5×5=2416.5+1.5\times5=24. The multiplier 1.5 is a chosen screening convention, not a universally provable boundary between valid observations and mistakes. Different quartile conventions may shift the fence slightly.




Compare responsibly
If two groups have unequal sample sizes, raw histogram or dotplot counts can be visually misleading for percentage comparisons. Use relative-frequency histograms with common bin boundaries when the investigative question concerns proportions; keep the number of observations and graph units visible. When two distributions have different numerical units (for example, exam grades out of different totals), raw values cannot be directly compared until their meanings are put on a common scale.
A stronger AP response names both groups, the quantitative variable, the units, and numerical or graphical evidence supporting the comparison. Describing does not establish causation; study design determines whether causal conclusions are justified. More guidance on design follows in Topics 1.10–1.13.

Checkpoint. If two boxplots have identical medians but one has a wider box, what can you conclude? Its middle 50% has a larger IQR. You cannot conclude which one has more peaks or which group always has larger observations. Explain why.

3 · Relative position: the z-score
A score of 86 on one assessment and 90 on another does not say which is stronger relative to its own distribution. The reference mean and standard deviation provide the missing context. A z-score gives the number of standard deviations an observation lies above or below its reference mean.
For a population with mean μ\mu and standard deviation σ>0\sigma>0,
z=x−μσ.
z=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}.

Here xx is the observed value. Subtracting the mean gives a distance in the original units; dividing by σ\sigma converts it into standard-deviation units. A z-score is unit-free: positive above the mean, negative below it, and zero at the mean.


Derivation: distance in standard-deviation units (optional)

If an observation is zz standard deviations above the mean, its displacement is zσz\sigma. Thus
x−μ=zσ⇒z=x−μσ.
x-\mu=z\sigma\quad\Longrightarrow\quad z=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}.

The numerator and denominator share the same measurement units, so the units cancel. The condition σ>0\sigma>0 matters: with no variability, this standardized distance is undefined.


Worked example: compare two assessments
On Assessment A, a student scores 86 points. The population mean is 70 points and its standard deviation is 8 points:
zA=86−708=168=2.00.
z_A=\frac{86-70}{8}=\frac{16}{8}=\boxed{2.00}.

On Assessment B, the student scores 90 points. The population mean is 80 points and its standard deviation is 10 points:
zB=90−8010=1010=1.00.
z_B=\frac{90-80}{10}=\frac{10}{10}=\boxed{1.00}.

Assessment A has the stronger relative position: two standard deviations above its own mean, compared with one on B, even though its raw score is lower.


Interpret signs and compare distributions
A z-score of −1.5-1.5 means one and a half standard deviations below the reference mean; +2+2 means two standard deviations above it. Whether a larger value is desirable depends on the variable: a higher assessment score might be desirable, while a longer emergency wait time might not.
A z-score describes standardized distance, not a percentile or probability. Equal z-scores in differently shaped distributions can correspond to different percentile ranks. Standardizing preserves shape and ordering; it does not make a distribution normal.


Recover a value from its z-score
Rearrange the standardization formula:
x=μ+zσ.
x=\mu+z\sigma.



Derivation: recover the raw value (optional)

Multiply both sides of z=(x−μ)/σz=(x-\mu)/\sigma by σ\sigma, then add μ\mu:
zσ=x−μ,x=μ+zσ.
\begin{aligned}
z\sigma&=x-\mu,\\
x&=\mu+z\sigma.
\end{aligned}

For example, z=1.5z=1.5, μ=70\mu=70 points and σ=8\sigma=8 points give x=70+1.5(8)=82x=70+1.5(8)=82 points.



Describe relative position within a sample
Use the sample’s own mean x‾\bar{x} and sample standard deviation s>0s>0:
zsample=x−x‾s.
z_{\mathrm{sample}}=\frac{x-\bar{x}}{s}.



Why use the sample summaries?

This defines relative position using the sample’s own center and spread. Sample summaries estimate population parameters when the sampling context supports that use; they are not automatically equal to them. State which reference group the standardized score describes.

In Route A’s sample, a 21-minute trip has
zA=21−16.52.393≈1.88.
z_A=\frac{21-16.5}{2.393}\approx1.88.

In Route B’s sample, a 19-minute trip has
zB=19−15.5837.633≈0.45.
z_B=\frac{19-15.583}{7.633}\approx0.45.

The Route A trip is farther above its own route’s mean in standard-deviation units. Percentile comparisons would also require the shapes of the distributions.


Z-score explorer: predict, change, compare
Before changing any inputs, predict: if the population SD for Assessment B were smaller while its mean and observed score stayed fixed, would the B z-score increase or decrease?

The entire lesson in one comparison: use a common-scale graph to understand shape, center, spread, and unusual features. Use a numerical summary to quantify evidence. Use a z-score when the question concerns an individual’s relative distance from their reference mean. Never substitute a z-score for a complete description or an experimental design.

text:
Common errors and final checklist

Compare like with like. Name both groups, use the same variable and units, and use common scales. For unequal sample sizes, use relative frequencies when comparing proportions.
Describe more than the average. Compare center, spread, shape and unusual features. Name the statistic or graphical feature supporting each claim.
Choose a graph for the feature. Dotplots and histograms reveal gaps and peaks; boxplots summarize quartiles, median and spread. A boxplot alone does not establish normality or the number of modes.
Interpret z-scores in their reference groups. Use a positive standard deviation and explain the sign and magnitude. Standardized distance is not a percentile, and standardization does not create normality.
Match conclusions to the evidence. Descriptive displays show sample patterns; population and causal conclusions depend on study design.

Question 1Two classes recorded daily screen time in minutes. Class X has 20
students and Class Y has 80. Which graph best compares the shapes of the

A. Two histograms of raw frequency, one with 5-minute bins and one with
20-minute bins.
B. Two bar charts of class names showing the number of students.
C. Two relative-frequency histograms with equal 5-minute bins on a
common time axis.
D. Two pie charts showing just each class’s total minutes.
Show solutionC. Relative-frequency histograms use the same measurement, common bin
boundaries and relative heights, so group size does not determine the
bar heights.

Question 2Route A has 12 journey times with median 16.5 minutes, IQR 3 minutes
and a fairly balanced dotplot. Route B has 12 times with median 13.5
minutes, IQR 5 minutes and a pronounced high right tail, including 38
minutes. Write a three-sentence comparison containing center,
variability and one feature of shape or unusual observations.
Show solutionRoute B’s sample median journey time is 3 minutes shorter (13.5
versus 16.5), but its middle-half journey times vary more (IQR 5 versus
3 minutes). Route B has a long right tail and unusually high 38-minute
trip, whereas A is more balanced. These observations describe the
sampled trips only; they do not show that riding B causes a shorter
trip.
Award credit for named groups and minutes, correct median
comparison/difference, correct IQR comparison, justified tail or outlier
feature, and no unsupported causal claim.

minutes. By how many minutes is A’s median LONGER than B’s? Enter a
positive number.
Show solution16.5−13.5=316.5-13.5=3
minutes. This is the difference between sample medians, not a statement
about every individual’s journey.

Question 7A student scores 86 on Assessment A (population mean 70, SD 8) and 90
on Assessment B (population mean 80, SD 10). Which statement compares
the relative positions correctly?
A. The score on A is farther above its reference mean in SD units.
B. The score on B has a higher z-score because 90 > 86.

zA=2z_A=2
and

Question 8Two reference populations both have mean 50 and standard deviation
10, but one is strongly right-skewed while the other is approximately
symmetric. A score of 60 has
z=1z=1
in both. Does this prove that 60 is at the same percentile in both
populations? Explain.
Show solutionNo. Both scores are 10 units above their respective mean, which is
one standard deviation in each population. But a percentile is
determined by the shape of each entire distribution—the fraction of
observations at or below 60. Different shapes can give different
cumulative proportions at the same z-score; z-scoring does not transform
either distribution to normal.
Correctly state no, recognize both standardized distances equal +1,
explain that percentile depends on cumulative distribution shape and
cannot be inferred from mean and SD alone.

Question 9A population has mean 60 points and population SD 4 points. What RAW
score has
z=−1.5z=-1.5?

Question 10Someone reads the two route samples and writes: ‘Because Route B’s
median is three minutes shorter, switching everyone from A to B will
cause each person’s travel time to drop by three minutes.’ Explain TWO
logically separate problems with this claim, and state a supported
descriptive conclusion.
Show solutionFirst, a difference between sample medians is a comparison of group
summaries, not a three-minute saving for every rider—journey times
overlap and vary substantially. Second, without an appropriate
randomized or otherwise justified causal design, observed groups cannot
show that changing routes causes a reduction. Supported descriptive
claim: in the two samples, B’s median is 13.5 minutes compared with A’s

title: Topic 1.10 The Investigative Question Revisited and Data Collection
text:
1. Turn curiosity into a statistical question
A statistical investigation begins before the first graph is drawn. We must decide what information would answer the question, from whom it should be collected, and what conclusions the design can justify. Consider a school that wants to know whether a short morning mathematics review improves students’ next quiz scores.
“Does review help?” is too vague to investigate. Who is being studied? What counts as “help”? Will students choose whether to attend, or will the school assign sessions? A useful investigative question has three linked components.
Variables and population. Specify the observational units, explanatory and response variables when relevant, and the population of interest. Here the observational unit might be one grade 10 student, with next quiz score (points) as the quantitative response variable.
Statistical purpose. Decide whether the aim is to estimate a population characteristic, compare groups, or evaluate a claim about a parameter. An estimate of the proportion willing to attend is different from a test of whether assigned review increases the population mean score.
Intended conclusion. Identify the group to which results should apply and whether the claim is descriptive, associational or causal. Study design limits conclusions even when observed differences are large.
A population parameter summarizes a population; a sample statistic summarizes the measured sample. If pp denotes the proportion of all current grade 10 students willing to attend, the sample proportion p̂\hat p can help estimate it. A confidence interval seeks a plausible range for pp. The calculation will be developed in a later unit, but the target parameter must be clear now.
For a hypothesis test about the assigned review experiment, let μR\mu_R denote the population mean score under the review condition and μN\mu_N the population mean under no review. The directional question is expressed by
H0:μR−μN=0versusHa:μR−μN>0.
H_0:\mu_R-\mu_N=0
\quad\text{versus}\quad
H_a:\mu_R-\mu_N>0.
The null hypothesis H0H_0 represents no mean difference; the alternative HaH_a represents higher mean performance under review. A different question—whether the means differ in either direction—would use Ha:μR−μN≠0H_a:\mu_R-\mu_N\ne0. Declaring a hypothesis is not evidence that it is true.

Why these hypotheses? — definition and rationale


The contrast μR−μN\mu_R-\mu_N represents the difference between population means. Equality corresponds to a difference of zero; the claim that review increases the mean corresponds to a positive difference. The sign is chosen to match the investigative question. These are definitions of competing claims, not a theorem requiring a proof.

text:
2. Population, census and sample
The population is the entire group the question targets. A census records the variable for every member of that group; a sample records it for some members. If a school has 240 grade 10 students, recording all 240 is a census of that school’s current grade 10 population, but not of every student in the district. Recording 60 of the 240 is a sample.
A census need not be perfect: nonresponse and measurement errors remain possible. Likewise, a large sample is not necessarily representative if the selection process systematically excludes some people. The procedures for random sampling and sampling bias are examined in Topics 1.11 and 1.12.
Check your understanding. A researcher asks every student in one school’s basketball team about sleep. This is a census of that team, but is not a census of all students at the school.

title: Topic 1.10 The Investigative Question Revisited and Data Collection
text:
3. Observational studies and experiments
The most important distinction is whether the researcher imposes a treatment, not whether the researcher collects numerical data, follows people over time, or asks for volunteers.

Observational studies
An observational study records naturally occurring variables without assigning the explanatory conditions. Investigators could ask students whether they voluntarily attend review sessions and compare their later quiz scores. Attending may be related to score, but this design by itself does not isolate a causal effect of review.
A survey is an observational study that collects answers from people using a standard set of questions. A prospective study selects its observational units at a point in time and gathers information then and into the future, whereas a retrospective study selects units now and gathers information from the past, perhaps using records. Both can be observational: simply observing people for many months does not turn a study into an experiment.
A confounding variable provides an alternative explanation for an observed association. Prior mathematics preparation might affect both students’ decision to attend review and their quiz scores. It is a plausible confounder because it relates to both the explanatory and response variables, not merely because it affects scores.

  Prior preparation
  ↙      ↘
  Voluntary review attendanceQuiz score
  The observed attendance–score association may have an alternative explanation.



Experiments
An experiment deliberately assigns conditions, called treatments, to experimental units and measures outcomes. The experimental unit is the smallest unit receiving a treatment; if individuals receive it, they may be called subjects or participants. For a review-session experiment where students are assigned separately, each student is an experimental unit.
A factor is an explanatory variable deliberately manipulated; its different settings are levels. The treatment is a factor level or a combination of levels across factors. In a two-factor experiment with review (yes/no) and practice format (paper/digital), there are four treatments, not two:




Paper practice
Digital practice




Assigned review
Review + paper
Review + digital


No review
No review + paper
No review + digital



The response variable is the observed outcome measured after treatment, for example next-quiz score in points. Treatment assignment and the response are different variables.
Random assignment uses chance to allocate treatments among units. It makes systematic selection into treatment groups less likely and supports a cause-and-effect interpretation when the rest of the experiment is sound. It does not guarantee that the groups are identical on every characteristic.
Random selection, in contrast, uses chance to choose observational units from the target population. Random selection addresses to whom results may be generalized; random assignment addresses whether a treatment caused an observed difference. A volunteer experiment can randomly assign treatments without randomly sampling the wider population.

Ask two separate questions: How did participants enter the study? and How were treatments allocated? For sound designs with appropriate measurement and response rates, these decisions give the following broad guidance.








Randomly selected from target population?
Treatments randomly assigned?
Appropriate conclusion

No
Yes
A causal comparison can apply to participants and similar people, but not automatically to the entire population.


No
No
Describe participants and observed associations; broad generalization and causal claims are limited.



In an observational study no treatment is assigned, so the random-assignment question does not apply. Some experiments impose treatments without random assignment; pre-existing differences may then undermine a causal conclusion.

Try these cases and explain the difference: (1) randomly select students but observe naturally occurring attendance; (2) invite volunteers and randomly assign review; (3) randomly select students and randomly assign review. The first supports population descriptions, the second helps assess a causal effect among people like the volunteers, and the third can support both conclusions, subject to the study’s other conditions.


Further design considerations


Randomization does not repair poor measurement, substantial nonresponse, failure to follow assigned conditions, or serious attrition. Ethical research requires informed consent as appropriate, privacy safeguards, accurate recording, reasonable risk, and fair treatment of participants. Sometimes an experimental treatment would be unethical or infeasible; an observational investigation may then be the suitable design.

title: Topic 1.10 The Investigative Question Revisited and Data Collection
text:
5. Worked AP exam example
The released 2024 AP Statistics Free-Response Question 3 asks students to distinguish an observational car-mileage study from a randomized driving comparison, then evaluate generalization. Read the original question directly below, followed by its worked explanation.










College Board · 2024 AP Statistics · Question 3, pp. 7–8.




Accessible text summary of the original question


Researchers ask owners of four car models to estimate gas mileage. A Model D owner, James, then compares mileage on 70 commuting days, randomly assigning autopilot to 35 days and manual driving to the other 35. Finally he asks whether the result applies to all Model D cars in his club.


Part (a): This is an observational study, because researchers record existing car ownership and mileage without assigning car models to people.
Part (b): Label the 70 commuting days 11 through 7070. Use a random-number generator to select 35 distinct labels without replacement; those days receive autopilot driving, while the other 35 receive manual driving. This randomly assigns two treatments to days (the experimental units). Merely alternating days would not be random.
Part (c): James’s car was not randomly sampled from the Model D club’s cars. To generalize to the club’s population, he should randomly select club-owned Model D cars and conduct a suitable experiment on those sampled cars. Random assignment of treatment days cannot substitute for random selection of cars.
The lesson of the question is to describe selection and assignment in different sentences before making a population or causal claim.

6. Synthesis
Before collecting data, check the target population and observational units; the variables to be measured; whether the goal is estimation, testing or association; whether the study is a census, observational investigation or experiment; any assignment and selection mechanisms; plausible confounders; and the ethical and practical limits of the conclusions.

text:
Practice

Loading practice…

Question 1A school plans to compare students assigned 15 minutes versus 25
minutes of lunch. Which question clearly identifies a response and a
population?
A. Is the lunchroom pleasant?
B. Among students at this school, does mean food waste per student
(grams) differ between the assigned lunch periods?
C. Does the principal like lunch?
D. Are longer lunches good?
Show solutionB. The response is grams of food discarded per student and the
population is students at this school; assigned lunch duration is the
explanatory factor.

Question 2All 240 current grade 10 students at one school report last night’s
sleep duration. Relative to that school’s grade 10 population this
is
A. a census
B. a simple random sample
C. a convenience sample
D. a randomized experiment
Show solutionA. All 240 current grade 10 students are included; it is a census of
that specific population, not of the whole district.

Question 3Researchers record existing phone brands and customers’ satisfaction
ratings without changing the phones used. The research is
A. a completely randomized experiment
B. a matched-pairs experiment
C. an observational study
D. a stratified random sample by design
Show solutionC. Researchers measured naturally occurring ownership and responses;
no brand treatment was assigned.

Question 4Researchers select people today, measure activity now, and collect
blood-pressure outcomes in subsequent years. They never assign an
exercise program. This is best described as
A. a randomized experiment
B. a prospective observational study
C. a retrospective observational study
D. a census
Show solutionB. The study follows participants into the future and does not impose
treatments, so it is prospective and observational.

Question 5Researchers recruit adults now and inspect medical records from the
past ten years; no treatment is imposed. What type of study is this?
A. retrospective observational study
B. prospective experiment
C. randomized experiment
D. factorial experiment
Show solutionA. Data are drawn from past records, so the observational study is
retrospective.

Question 6A researcher assigns each student either 10 or 20 minutes of
mathematics review, then measures a 20-point quiz. Identify the
experimental units, explanatory variable, factor levels, treatments, and
response variable.
Show solutionEach student is an experimental unit; review duration is the
explanatory factor, with levels 10 and 20 minutes, which are also the
two treatments. The response is that student’s quiz score, measured out
of 20 points.
Identify the relevant units or population; state an accurate design
classification; justify the conclusion using selection, assignment or
possible confounding; avoid unsupported causal or population claims.

Question 7Students who voluntarily participate in a study club have a higher
average test score than nonmembers. Describe a plausible confounder and
explain why the data do not establish that the club caused better
scores.
Show solutionPrior academic preparation or motivation could influence both the
choice to join the club and test scores. Because membership was not
randomly assigned, the association could partly reflect those
pre-existing differences. A higher mean alone cannot establish a causal
club effect.
Identify the relevant units or population; state an accurate design
classification; justify the conclusion using selection, assignment or
possible confounding; avoid unsupported causal or population claims.

Question 8A simple random sample of students is surveyed about existing sleep
habits and scores, without assigning any sleep schedule. Which claim is
most defensible?
A. The study proves additional sleep causes higher scores.
B. A random sample makes this a randomized experiment.
C. The study cannot describe sleep and scores in the population.
D. With sound measurement and response, the sample may describe a
population association, but causal conclusions are limited.
Show solutionD. Random selection supports population generalization; observing
habits without imposing treatment does not establish causation.

Question 9Twenty self-selected volunteers are randomly assigned to receive a
study aid or no aid. What is the strongest warranted conclusion under an
otherwise sound experiment?
A. The results generalize automatically to all students in the
province.
B. Differences can support a causal effect for participants like these
volunteers, not automatic generalization to the whole province.
C. No causal conclusion can ever follow from volunteer participants.
D. Random assignment proves identical treatment groups in every
characteristic.
Show solutionB. Random treatment assignment can justify causal comparisons among
comparable volunteers, while the nonrandom recruitment limits wider
generalization.

Question 10A district wants to know whether an online tutoring service improves
grade 10 mathematics achievement throughout the district. Propose an
investigative question, identify a relevant outcome, explain how to
select participants and allocate treatments, and describe the
conclusions your design could justify.
Show solutionQuestion: Among district grade 10 students, is the population mean
score on a common mathematics assessment higher for those assigned
access to tutoring than for those assigned usual instruction? Select
eligible students at random from the district and, with appropriate
consent and school safeguards, randomly assign selected students to
tutoring access or comparison. Measure the common assessment
consistently. Random selection supports generalization to the sampled
district population; random assignment supports a causal treatment
comparison if implementation and follow-up are sound.
Identify the relevant units or population; state an accurate design
classification; justify the conclusion using selection, assignment or
possible confounding; avoid unsupported causal or population claims.




Sources
